Rede um die zukünftige Zollpolitik Englands anhören konnten. Rede Chamberlains im Parlament am 28.5.1903. Trade and the empire Speeches by Mr Balfour and Mr. Chamberlain. On the motion for the adjournment for the Whitsun recess, Sir C. Dilke said it was impossible for the House to adjourn without reference being made to topics which had recently been introduced as electoral topics for the consideration of the country on behalf of the Administration, constituting a change in their fiscal policy so complete and so revolutionary, and so opposed to all the traditions and, he believed, the opinions of the overwhelming majority of members of that House, as to make it a matter of urgent importance. The declarations were those made in recent speeches by the Colonial Secretary and Mr. Bonar Law. At the time he did not think the speech of Mr. Chamberlain on the 15th inst. carried matters much further than the right hon. gentleman had carried them some years ago, but in the light of the speech made in debate on Friday last, and read in the light of the direst statement of Mr. Law, the matter assumed momentous importance. The Colonial Secretary dotted the i’s of his first speech when he stated that the money, which must be a very large sum, for old-age pensions could not be supplied except by one means –duties on foreign imports into this country. There, he thought, he pointed to a duty on food and raw materials. Mr. Chamberlain: No. Sir C. Dilke could not conceive how, unless duties were laid on food and raw materials, they could obtain the money necessary. Mr. Chamberlain: I shall have to explain at some length in order to put my position before the House, but I would now ack the right hon. Baronet not to quote me as having been committed to this, that, and the other proposition. (Opposition laughter.) I am afraid I have not made myself quite clear. I have not the slightest objection to the right hon. baronet quoting me to any extent he likes. What I mean is that he must not appeal to me to agree with him. That is all. (Ministerial cheers.) Sir C. Dilke said the main words used by Mr. Chamberlain were that a vast sum was to be provided by a review of their fiscal system, and it could not be denied that they must be read in connection with a general system of duties on foreign imports. His contention was that it was impossible to find that amount of money without imposing duties on food and raw materials. That the Colonial Secretary must have been thinking of some system of the kind was clear from another speech and in the letter in which he stated that the working classes would, in his belief, submit to a considerable raising of the cost of living for themselves provided they got increased wages as a result. Surely that pointed to duties all round, and not to duties on luxuries. Mr. Law’s speech took the speeches entirely out of the category of personal utterances. He stated, as though by authority, that the speeches were concerted together by the Government. Mr. B. Law dissented. Sir C. Dilke said the hon. gentleman referred not only to the speeches of Mr. Chamberlain but to recent utterances of Mr. Balfour and Mr. Long, and stated “the speakers struck the same note. They struck it in complete harmony. Anyone might see what was the actual fact, that the policy expressed in those speeches was a policy arranged beforehand between the statesmen who uttered them?" (Opposition cheers.) He wished to know whether Mr. Bonar Law spoke at Chester with the authority of the financial department of the Government which was specially concerned. Even the Prime Minister could not assume the assent of his colleagues to so startling a change in our fiscal policy. (Opposition cheers.) He should have thought, from the constitutional uses of this country, that the question was one which should have come before and been settled by the Cabinet as a whole. The Government, of course, were parties to the Colonial conferences of 1881 and 1902, which were called to consider the defence contribution from the Colonies, and after that to consider whether preference should be given to the Mother Country by the Colonies. From the contribution point of view these conferences turned out a fiasco, but the conference of 1897 did produce the adoption by Canada of preferential duties in our favour. The Secretary of State had said the effect of the preferential duties was to make the rate of increase under the preferential tariff less than the general rate of increase under the free tariff. That was a pretty admission! (Opposition cheers.) The Secretary to the Board of Trade, who was a sort of professional economist to the Government, and who was always turned on to put a kind of economic gloss over the Government heresies – (laughter) knew that this was their weak point. But he tackled it courageously in that speech at Chester. The hon- gentleman, who was a Canadian Protectionist, said that he had carefully examined the figures and that he was well within the mark in saying we had at least 20 per cent. more trade with Canada than we would have had if preference had not been granted. This was highly hypothetical. (Laughter.) It was said there was concurrence among the leading members of the Government as to large duties on imports; but the abolition of the corn-tax did not confirm that statement. (Opposition cheers.) The Chancellor of the Exchequer was suspected of heresy, but he was a tower of strength to Free Trade, although he had a past. (Opposition laughter.) The Chancellor of the Exchequer was like the late Archbishop of Canterbury, whose first preferment to a bishopric caused the clergy to rise in arms, but who ended by being the defender of orthodoxy. (Opposition cheers.) Fres traders gladly took Mr. Ritchie to their arms, trusting he would stick to his present views. (Opposition cheers.) The speech of the Colonial Secretary a fortnight ago must be regarded as the foundation of this policy. The right hon. gentleman said if Cobden were alive he would have been on his platform. (Opposition laughter.) It was equally easy to say that Cobden if alive might have been a Salvationist. (Laughter.) Nobody could tell; but if he were in favour of the Colonial Secretary's new policy it could only be from excessive age, leading to softening of the brain. The Colonial Secretary said that the idea of common responsibility by the various parts of the Empire was (recognised in the foundation of all Colonies in the Tudor and Stuart days. There was a astounding omission in the right hon. Gentleman’s Birmingham speech, one which robbed the policy set forth in that speech of all claim to be Imperial. The Colonial Secretary left entirely out of account the four hundred millions of his Majesty's coloured subjects. There was no vestige of a suggestion as to how the enormous Indian problem was to be faced. India paid her share of the cost of running the Empire, while the Colonies did not pay. (Opposition cheers.) Trade preferences had been tried before, and it was admitted to be a gigantic failure. What Australia had suggested was merely “a preference not yet defined as to nature or extent”, and Lord Tennyson had declared in the name of the Commonwealth Ministry that, while they agreed to these general words, they were not in a position to make any proposals to Parliament on the subject. Therefore, as there was not the faintest chance of any such proposal being made to the Commonwealth Parliament, it was most unwise and rash, unless it was done for domestic or election reasons, to raise the question at this time. Three years ago the Colonial Secretary had declared the difficulties to be insuperable. What had happened since that this question should be forced upon the country? (Opposition cheers.) Mr. Chamberlain in 1900 had said that if there was to be any kind would be viewed with the slightest favour in this country would be a Zollverein, in which there would be Free Trade within the Empire. Of course, that would be impossible, for Australia would not look at it. Protection in Australia was directed against us, against our manufactures, and against the cheap labour of India; and that protection she could not afford to abolish. He agreed with the Colonial Secretary that nothing else than an Imperial Zollverein had the slightest chance of being considered in this country. We received nearly the whole of our cotton and an enormous amount of beef, most of our mineral oil – the light of the poor – and an enormous proportion of the half-manufactured goods on which our industries depended from North and South America. Were we to jeopardise such a trade and tax the food of the people and the cotton that comes here for manufacturing for the purpose of bolstering up the small producers in our own Colonies? He was convinced that this policy had not been thought out, and when it was it would be as universally condemned as in the time of our fathers and grandfathers. Mr. Balfour: I do not think there is much with which I am in sympathy in the speech we have just listened to, but, at all events, I agree that the present is a more convenient occasion for raising this discussion than the second reading of the Budget Bill. Though the right hon. gentleman had a large and important audience, I am sorry that there were not numbered in his audience the leaders of the party to which he belongs. (Loud Ministerial cheers.) There was one word which recurred at brief intervals throughout the right hon. baronet's speech, and that was the word “heresy" —a word of theological importance, which I do not think is dealing with questions of this kind. I would urge the House, in dealing with this question, not to wave the flags, somewhat ragged and moth-eaten, which have been in use, either on the Protectionist or Free Trade side, in a controversy which I think, at all events, is removed far as the poles asunder from the great debates in which our fathers were engaged forty-odd years ago. The right hon. baronet, in a part of his speech, endeavoured to discuss in a serious spirit the very difficult problem on which we are now engaged and another part of his speech was devoted to the less elevating object of attempting to make mischief between my right hon. friend (Hr. Chamberlain) and myself. In that amiable intention I think the right hon. gentlemen will fail – (Ministerial cheers)– and may I ask him what course he thinks my right hon. friend ought to have pursued in this matter after what occurred at the Colonial Conference last year? The Colonial Prime Ministers were asked to come to this country, and when in this country they were asked to confer with the Secretary of State for the Colonies and other high officers of the Government upon questions material to the Empire as a whole. They did engage in this discussion, and the result of their labours is embodied in the Blue Book. One conclusion which the Prime Ministers endorsed was this: “ That this conference recognises that the principle of preferential trade (between the United Kingdom and his Majesty’s dominions beyond the sea would stimulate mutual commercial intercourse, and would, by promoting the development of the resources of industry of its several parts, strengthen the Empire.“ I want to know whether, in Sir O. Dilke’s opinion, and in the opinion of the House and the country, the Colonial Secretary, who summoned that conference, and whose personal influence and genius have done so much to stimulate a feeling of common citizenship in all parts of the Empire – (Ministerial cheers) – ought to have allowed that resolution of the Prime Ministers to sleep in the pages of a Blue Book, or whether he was not bound to raise the subject for discussion and decision, not merely by the people of our country, but by the peoples of all parts of the Empire. (Ministerial cheers.) I do not see that he had any choice, and if he did it with characteristic force and genius, surely that is no ground for making any complaint of the policy, if complaint is to be made at all. I should like the House to take a rather wider, more general, and certainly a less polemical view of the present fiscal position of this country than has been taken by Sir C. Dilke. He has been constantly referring to the old Free Trade controversies, and repeating the old Free Trade formulas. These formulas, like all scientific formulas, are accurate within the limits of the facts to which they refer. I will not say that I am a Free Trader – I don’t wish to treat this thing by bandying titles across the floor of the House, but to treat it in a serious, sober, and scientific spirit. The position of these islands is now entirely different, not only from what it was in 1848 but from what the Free Traders of that date supposed it would be. (Ministerial cheers.) They thought – and I think the prophecy was a very natural one – that our example would induce the whole world to adopt a Free Trade policy, and that this country would find itself a Free Trade nation among Free Trade nations. But their prophecies, unfortunately were wrong. (Hear, hear.) There is absolutely now in the whole world not one civilised Free Trade community except ourselves. I do not think that any observer of contemporary tendencies will suggest for one instant that the policy in which every civilised community, including our self-governing Colonies, has thus embarked, is a policy which they show the smallest inclination to reverse. (Hear, hear.) We have, therefore, to look forward to a condition of things in which more and more there will be a wall of hostile tariffs built up against us, in which foreign nations will use their power of manipulating their own tariffs to our disadvantage, and in which we shall be less and less able to find in civilised countries a market for our manufactured goods. (Ministerial cheers.) Take the case of Russia, which, in one sense, is highly Protectionist, and which, from the necessities of its situation, is obliged to take a large amount of our manufactured goods. The deliberate policy of the Russian Minister of Finance is so to manipulate the tariff that gradually Russia shall become what America has long aspired to be – an industrially selfcontained community. If that tendency is to go on at the present rate—and who will be rash enough to say that it is not going on?—the time must come when the only neutral markets, as they are called, will be the Turkish Empire, our own Protectorates, our own Crown Colonies, and India. This country will then be in a position—and it is now tending towards that position—in which it is obliged to import an enormous proportion of its foodstuffs and raw materials, und will have to pay for them by exports which it will find extremely difficult and onerous to dispose of in any of the countries which I have described. The old Protectionist idea was that it was your business, by excluding rival manufacturers, to foster your own manufactures. That is not my argument. What I am trying to point out is that, inasmuch as this country must more and more be a manufacturing, as opposed to an agricultural country, and must more and more depend upon foreign countries for its supplies of food, for which it will have to pay by exports, if we are compelled by exterior tariffs, whether in our own Colonies or foreign countries, to dispose of our exports on very onerous terms, it will mean an enormous loss not only to the manufacturers, but to the country as a whole (Ministerial cheers.) That effect is at present disguised –and may it long be disguised –by the fact that we have enormous investments abroad, and therefore it is comparatively easy for us to get our food supplies not merely by exporting our manufactures, but owe us as investors with their funds. But I confess that as far as I understand the modern tendencies of industry there is now a stream running the other way, and at all events as far as the United States are concerned-at one time one of our heaviest debtors – there is a movement in precisely the opposite direction, a movement which seems almost to tend in the direction of making us the debtors of the United States. I would impress on the House that this is not a Protectionist argument, and that it is a perfectly sound one. (Opposition laughter.) I do not say that the tendency justifies the policy of the Colonial Minister or any other policy – (hear, hear) – but I do say that it is a contingency which it is difficult to contemplate without alarm, and that policy has the undoubted recommendation that it does something, to mitigate the evils which I believe are undoubted, and which we may have to face at no distant period. (Ministerial cheers.) I would ask whether it should be excluded from public controversy—I don’t put it higher than that whether the time has not come when we must abandon, as an obsolete doctrine, the doctrine that revenue is never to be raised except for purposes of expenditure, and whether we are not bound in self-defence to contemplate the possibility of having to raise revenue for purposes other than national expenditure. Every other nation does it. I am enough of an Englishman to say that the unanimity of the world against us on this question of theory does not greatly perturb us – (Opposition cheers) – and I notice that gentlemen opposite are very much perturbed even another subject is mentioned. (Hear, hear; and laughter.) That, however, is not a matter I propose to go into, but I ask whether the time has not come when we may debate with advantage the possibility that taxation should be raised, not merely for purposes of dealing with national expenditure, but for other purposes. For example, are we really in our hearts content with a position which leaves us absolutely helpless in the face of all foreign countries with regard to tariff negotiations? (Hear, hear.) I do not think anyone likes the situation. They may say it is better than any remedy that might be proposed, but that in itself it is disagreeable will be admitted by anybody who has ever had to negotiate a tariff treaty with any foreign country. I go even further, and say that, if there is really to be an attempt on the part of foreign countries to declare that we are so separate from our self-governing Colonies that they may justily be trusted as separate nations, we must, we shall be forced by patriotism by public opinion, by every regard for ourselves and our Colonies, to resist that, and, if need be, to resist it by fiscal retaliation. (Cheers.) Are we really to be told by anybody that Canada, Australia, New Zealand, und India are not parts of the British Empire, that they are to be treated as separate nations simply because we have given them self-government? I quite admit that we, and we alone, so far as I know amongst the nations of the world, have been able to create such a thing as a loyal self-governing colony, but because we, und we alone, have been able to create such a thing are those self-governing Colonies to be excluded from the benefits which are given to the colonies of nations under the absolute control of their central administration? I am quite sure we should never assent to that, and yet I am equally sure it cannot be adequately resisted unless we have at our command some fiscal weapon by which those who thus seek to endeavour to disintegrate the Empire by fiscal means may be properly resisted. (Ministerial cheers.) There is a second reason for which, I think, we may properly raise revenues for non-revenue purposes, and that is, in the words of the Colonial Prime Ministers, to bind the Empire closer together. Hon. gentlemen may say that that is a very good object, but not worth paying any large sum for. That is a thing which has to be debated, and I say you may well find out what it is you have to give and what it is you can get. The actual scheme the Prime Ministers desired was that there should be a preference given to imports from the Colonies in exchange for which they should mitigate the severity of their hostile tariffs against us. (Hear, hear.) Sir C. Dilke says such a tax must be a tax on raw material or food. I do not think il would be wise, under any circumstances, to tax the raw material required for any of the large manufactures. (Opposition cheers.) I am not aware that any proposal to tax raw materials has ever been put forward by any responsible person. Whether the people of this country would be willing to have their food taxed in order to gain these objects is not a thing on which Sir C. Dilke can speak with authority, and I cannot speak with authority either. If they are not willing, it would be impossible to carry out any large scheme which the Colonial Prime Ministers desired. (Opposition cheers.) l entirely agree with that. You will never, in my opinion, have a tax on food accepted by the people of this country, except as part of a great policy which they heartily and conscientiously accept. (Cheers.) The idea that you can go back to the old protective days and in the interests of this or that industry ask the people to tax their food is not, I think, within the region of practical politics. (Opposition cheers.) But does it follow from that that if by means of a tax on food you could put the whole fiscal und Imperial position of this country on a different and better feeting – is it so certain that the working class of this country would repudiate the suggestion? (Hear, hear.) Suppose that by a general tax upon food-stuffs it would be possible to stop this process by which, not merely in foreign countries, but in our own Colonies, there was being created not a system of protection but an enormous number of vested manufacturing interests – supposing it were possible by such a policy, not, indeed, to attain full free trade – for that is, I am afraid, beyond the power of any conceivable combination – but to attain a large measure of free trade in manufactured goods with the Colonies are you sure that that would not be worth while? (Hear, hear.) I am asked whether the working man would consent to any sacrifices. I do not know, and I ask a similar question about the Colonies, whether they would consent to make such a modification in their tariff system as has been suggested? Again, I say, I do not know, but unless you discuss the questions in this country and the Colonies how on earth can you arrive at a conclusion in the matter? (Hear, hear.) Of course, I admit that the two difficulties I have mentioned are greate – I mean the traditional objection of our population to a tax on food, and the traditional affection of the Colonies for a system of protection. These are two formidable things, and if you cannot overcome them you cannot have any plan of this kind. That is impossible, and no set of people would be more ready to admit it than the Colonial Prime Ministers, and nobody has stated it with more force than the Colonial Secretary. (Ministerial cheers.) I do not believe, if these difficulties were overcome, that there would be any, or hardly any, bad economic tendencies such as some gentlemen suggest. I always regret the manner in which political economy is treated in this House and on public platforms. It is not treated as a science, as a subject which we ought to approach impartially, with a view to real discovery what the truth is from theory or experience. The controversialists find a formula in some book or authority and throw it a their opponents’ heads. (laughter.) They bandy old watchwords and arouse old bitternesses wholly alien, as far as I can see, to any modern questions, and our controversies are thus apt to degenerate into outworn formulas imperfectly remembered and modern doctrines of political economy imperfectly understood. (Cheers und laughter.) That is a very unfortunate state of things, und I should hope that one result of my right hon friend's speech and the debate to day will be that the country will devote itself, not in a partisan spirit, to consider the real economic position in which we stand. May I say one word on a purely personal aspect of this question? My right hon. friend the Colonial Secretary has been accused, as I understand, of saying things in contradiction of, or inconsistent with, statements I have made; of having started a hare of his own and developed a policy of his own quite irrespective of his colleagues. I think I have shown, so far as I apprehend the matter, that there is no contradiction between my right hon. friend's views and my own. (Hear, hear.) But I go much further. Suppose my right hon. friend had done what he has not done, and formulated a policy of his own, without consulting his colleagues, I cannot understand on what ground criticism is to be levelled against him. Are my colleagues and I bound to come together and not merely consider whether we can act together as a united Government, but whether every speech is to be made with precisely the same, flavour of rhetoric about it? (Laughter.) The thing is absurd. Speaking for myself, I will not be a party to depriving others of a liberty which I have always arrogated to myself. (Ministerial cheer.) Some years ago I made speeches and wrote letters regarding university education in Ireland. Those were my own opinions. I did not bind the Government, or mean to bind the Government, to them. I thought, and I still think, great good might be done, and as a matter of fact it was done, by ventilating the question. If you prevent politicians who are or have been in high office from taking an independent line upon subjects which are not part of the momentary policy of the Government, you lose one of the most valuable methods of forming and directing public opinion. (Ministerial cheers.) You cannot leave, and you ought not to leave – Mr. CAUSTON (speaking to an hon. member on the bench behind): That is a new idea. Mr. BALFOUR: Does the hon. gentleman say it is a new idea? Then, if it is a new idea, it is a good one! (Ministerial laughter and cheers.) It is also a perfectly proper one. This question is not one that the House will have to decide this session, or next session, or the session after. It is not a question that this House will have to decide at all. It is not a question connected with this year’s Budget. It is a question of general fiscal policy which requires the most careful examination and study on its strictly economic and scientific side, and also on its Imperial and social side. (Opposition cheers.) How is that study to be even started or brought to any useful result if these imaginary bonds are to be drawn as tight as the hon. gentleman supposes? My right hon. friend, I believe, is in absolute agreement with everything I have said to-day. Mr. CHAMBERLAIN: Hear, hear. Mr. BALFOUR: Supposing he were not, and that on this point there was a difference of opinion between us, is that a reason why he should keep silence? Not at all! It would be an enormous loss to the really formative forces of this country and to the society in which we live if you prevent any man in public affairs having that freedom of expression on matters not immediately before the country or the, House which, no doubt, ultimately tend to the formation of a sane and well-instructed public opinion. (Ministerial cheers.) I know some of the arguments I have adduced have been dry, and, perhaps, not easy to follow, but I am convinced that the trend of thought I have ventured to develop, in, I believe, absolute conformity with the views of my right hon. Friend – (Mr. Chamberlain: Hear, hear) – is eminently worthy of consideration, not merely within these walls, not chiefly within these walls, but by public discussion, and by acquiring information, as we mean to acquire information, so far as we can. (Ministerial cheers.) Then, if public opinion ripens, if the Colonies and if the people of this country are of opinion that, we ought to do something to put the British Empire in an economic position which will make it in any way equal to the magnificent economic position obtained by the United States— (hear, hear)—I think we shall have done well. (Loud Ministerial cheers.) I am not certain that this scheme is practicable— (Opposition cheers)—but I am certain unless this scheme proves to be practicable, or unless some other scheme having the same results can be brought to fruition if the British Empire is to remain as it is at present, a series of isolated economic units – it is vain for us to hope that this branch, at all events, of the great Anglo-Saxon race is destined to have the great and triumphant economic progress which undoubtedly lies before the United States of America. (Loud Ministerial cheers.) Mr. LLOYD-GEORGE said that after listening very carefully to Mr. Balfour no one had the slightest impression as to what the policy of the Government was. The Prime Minister talked about not being responsible for the rhetoric of the Colonial Secretary. That was a very necessary disclaimer (laughter) but did he treat the speech of the right hon. gentleman merely as an exhibition of fireworks? (Opposition laughter and cheers.) The House ought to know that. The question was whether this was the practical policy which the Prime Minister was going to submit to the country. On Friday last the Colonial Secretary said old-age pensions were not dead. They were going to be dealt with. It was a practical matter at last. Mr. Chamberlain shook his head. Had it ceased to be a practical matter since Friday last? Mr. CHAMBERLAIN: I only shook my head in protest against the continued and most improper actions of the hon. gentleman who invariably misquotes me. Mr. LLOYD-GEORGE said he merely called the attention of the House to what happened on Friday. Mr. Chamberlain said that this matter was one to be dealt with by fiscal reform in this country. Mr. CHAMBERLAIN: I did not say what the hon. gentleman says I did. What I declared was that it could not be dealt with without a review of our fiscal policy. Mr. LLOYD-GEORGE recognised at once that there was a distinction. On Friday they understood there was a pledge to deal with old-age pensions; now they understood there was none. They ought to know whether it was a matter merely for debating societies and papers at the Colonial Institute or whether the Government were going to deal with it before they went out. Mr. BALFOUR: I do not know about going out; but we will not deal with it before the dissolution. (Loud laughter and Ministerial cheers.) Mr. LLOYD GEORGE, continuing, said that did not carry them much further. Were they going to have from Canada cheap cattle and cheap food for the people put in the same category as indecent literature? (Laughter.) Mr. BONAR LAW: I is not a question of decent or indecent literature, but of the prevention of the infringement of the British copyright law. Mr. LLOYD-GEORGE said twenty years ago Mr. Chamberlain made a speech in defence of Free Trade und against the tendencies of his Conservative opponents. He was so persuasive that the present Chancellor of the Exchequer became a free trader. It would be hard now if Mr. Ritchie were lured back upon his evil ways by the very missionary who was responsible for his conversion. (Opposition laughter.) In his speech of twenty years ago Mr. Chamberlain spoke about the new heterodoxy having secured the patronage of the Conservative party. Who would have thought that twenty years later the right hon. gentleman himself would be the patron saint? (Opposition laughter.) Lord H. CECIL expressed gratitude to the Prime Minister for his assurance that there would be no change in the policy of the Government before the dissolution of Parliament, because the question of Free Trade and Protection could not be shut out from discussion. (Opposition cheers.) It was absurd to speak, of heresy; at the same time heresy was not the same thing as a breach of scientific law. For many purposes the scientific law was a more awkward thing than heresy. (laughter.) An Arian might walk from top to bottom of the highest flight of steps, but a person who defied the law of gravitation would come to grief in the same enterprise. (laghter.) The fundamental principles laid down fifty years ago were in his opinion principles of a scientific character, and for that reason he was glad to learn that no attempt was for the present at least to be made to change them. (Opposition cheers.) He felt very strongly indeed that having regard to the political circumstances the ease against altering our fiscal system was very strong – (Opposition cheers)-because he was quite unable understand how an elaborate system of tariffs could be adjusted for the ostensible benefit of our Colonies without involving us in a series of delicate and difficult negotiations which would tend to throw the apple of discord between us and our brethren across the sea (Opposition cheers) – and which would therefore be from a political as well as a fiscal point of view a profound mistake. He desired to see the Empire drawn closer together, and he resented as strongly as any human being could the attitude of Germany with regard to Canadian preferential tariffs. They ought not even to seem to range themselves on the side of Mr. Lloyd-George, whose enthusiasm for the Empire was only less than his zeal for Church schools. Ministerial cheers and laughter.) He thought a political arrangement with the Colonies ought to precede any fiscal arrangement which might be possible. With regard to the very real grievance which Canada might feel against Germany, that there were many ways besides fiscal methods of expressing resentment at any ill-treatment of our Colonies. The friendship of this country was an asset, and opportunities ought to be taken to let foreign statesmen understand that the friendship of this country could not be more easily endangered than by an insult to our Colonies. If ten years hence some crisis arose in which the friendship of Britain was a great consideration to Germany, it would not be forgotten by the great body of the people of this country that Germany had not treated one of our Colonies with fairness and justice. (Cheers.) If these considerations were clearly brought home to Continental nations, he believed it would suffice to protect our Colonies from any such ill-treatment. Let those on that side of the House at least, as members of a great constitutional party, not hesitate to utter the belief in Free Trade which they had been in the habit of associating with the abounding prosperity of the country. (Cheers.) Mr. CHAMBERLAIN: I think we must all have observed that there is a certain unreality about this debate, because it has been carried on in the prospect and expectation of a still greater event. Notice has been given on behalf of the Leader of the party opposite of a discussion of this identical subject to take place on the second reading of the Finance Bill. Therefore, I suppose the present is only an affair of scouts, and that therefore gentlemen on the other side who have addressed us have been acting on behalf of their leaders as spies – (Opposition cries of "Oh!”) –-yes, spies in the military sense – a sort of military reconnaissance – to find out what are the weak points in our position. That prevents this debate from assuming the importance which the subject demands, but for my part should not think it wasted if it had only produced the speech to which we have just listened from Lord H. Cecil. (Cheers.) I should like to make one or two remarks about that very interesting, moderate, and suggestive speech. My noble friend has fallen into the error which seems to me to have been made by everyone who has spoken, with the exception of the Prime Minister – that a new policy has been proposed to the country, involving at a stroke an entire and absolute reversal of the whole fiscal policy of this country. I am absolutely unaware of any such proposal having been made either by myself or by anyone else, and before I sit down I hope to show how very much more limited is the suggestion which I have, not for the first time, but on several occasions during the last five or six years, put before the country. The second statement of my noble friend was that we were not hastily to deal with the fundamental propositions of that great historic doctrine which, in his judgment, has in its practical application done so much for the prosperity of this country. That doctrine is Free Trade, but my noble friend has failed, as everyone else has failed, to tell us what he means by Free Trade. Now, it is perfectly clear that everything depends upon the definition. I have always understood that Free Trade was that which would bring about a free interchange of commodities at their natural price. We are perfectly content to accept the interchange of commodities at their natural price, and I think we may go further, and ask that the definition should not in every case be strictly applied. But in our opinion there are certain deviations from this doctrine of Free Trade which we say necessitate the careful, and, in a sense, the immediate, attention of the country. My noble friend appealed to the traditions of the historic party with which he is connected, and sought to identify the Conservative party with (the doctrines of Free Trade. I do not know that that, can wholly be sustained –(laughter) – though no doubt Sir Robert Peel claimed to be a Conservative when he introduced Free Trade in corn. At all events, my noble friend is justified in saying that for a very long period that fundamental doctrine has been the doctrine of the party to which he belongs. That is not inconsistent with anything I have said in the speech which has formed the text of this discussion. It has been to me somewhat of a surprise to find that that speech has aroused exceptional attention, because there is nothing in it – except that rhetoric to which Mr. Lloyd-George so gracefully alluded – (laughter) – and which, no doubt, differs with his case and mine, and in the case of other orators – (renewed laughter)—which was not precisely the same in matter, substance, and suggestion as the speeches which were delivered on more than one occasion by Lord Salisbury, calling attention to precisely the dangers for which I have asked consideration. Nor does it differ from the speech made by the Prime Minister in his reply to the deputation that waited upon him with reference to the corn duty, nor from speeches which myself have made on the same subject during the last four or five years. However, I find that this greater interest is caused by an obiter dictum of mine, to the effect that it was quite possible that the issue at the next General Election would not be the issue which some hon. gentlemen have anticipated, but that it might be in connection with this very great, and, in my opinion, more important, subject. What does the Opposition want to get out of this debate? I judge from the speeches made that they want to know whether the Prime Minister and myself are in sharp disagreement. (Hear, hear.) They have had an answer – I do not know whether it was what they expected. (Ministerial laughter.) I wish, however, to say, in order that there may be no mistake as to my part in the matter, that I agree with every single word that fell from the Prime Minister – (Ministerial cheers) – and, as far as I know, there is no difference whatever of principle between, us in reference to it. (Renewed Ministerial cheers.) Mr. Lloyd-George, in a speech which really would have been humorous if it had been a little more good-natured (hear, hear) –asked if this question was to be discussed as a debating society matter. I answer that question in the negative. I do not think that the discussion to which we invite the House and the country is a debating society discussion. (Ministerial cheers.) It is much too serious really, as the hon. member will yet find out (Ministerial cheers)—for the very light treatment which he is inclined to give it. (Hear, hear.) Although nothing has been suggested in the nature of an entire reversal of the fiscal policy of the country, yet undoubtedly a new mandate would have to be given to the Government if the suggestions I have thrown out were to be carried into effect, and that new mandate will involve many considerations of the utmost importance, affecting not merely the prosperity of the country, not merely a general question as to the wealth of the country, but going deep into the condition of the working classes and their interests. Therefore, I do hope that in the great debate we are anticipating the subject will be treated as it was by Lord H. Cecil, with all the seriousness which it deserves. (Ministerial cheers.) Mr. Lloyd-George wishes to know whether the question will be raised at the dissolution. Sufficient unto the day. (Laughter.) In the meantime, he as well as others will no doubt have to discuss it in the country, and in regard to that, so far as I am concerned, I will do everything my limited power will permit to bring this question in all its bearings before the people of this country (Ministerial cheers.) Mr. LOUGH: What question? Mr. CHAMBERLAIN: I do not in the least object to the curiosity of the hon. member, but he need not be in such a hurry. (Laughter.) In the course of the debate somebody asked for a plan. If by a plan is meant a detailed scheme of some new tariff or new fiscal arrangement, or reciprocity treaty, nothing of the kind can be produced at the present moment. That is not the question I have raised, nor which has been raised by Lord Salisbury or the Prime Minister. What we have raised in effect is a principle. It is a question which we put to the people of this country. In my speech, if I may be permitted to refer to it, I called attention to what I considered the opportunity existing at the present time, and the importance of seizing the opportunity of making preferential arrangements in the nature of reciprocity agreement with our Colonies; and, in the second place, I called attention to the fact that under our existing system we were helpless and totally impotent to bring any influence to bear on foreign countries if they attacked our Colonies, or if they attacked us in any manner which we considered would be unfair or would seriously endanger our industry. As long as we can only say to them as we did to the Colonial Premiers last year, “ What you propose is against the fiscal system of this country,” so long as we have no weapons in our hands, we can not meet attacks upon our Colonies or upon ourselves, which are already serious, and which may become much more serious. (Ministerial cheers.) These were the two points which I brought before the country, and the question on which I invited discussion was, “Are you determined to maintain your interpretation of Free Trade with such severity that you refuse to give us power to meet these cases?" If that is the answer of the country, let us at once announce that answer to our Colonies, for nothing can be worse than to leave them in doubt. (Hear, hear.) Let us say to our Colonies, “No matter what you are prepared to do for us, no matter how much consideration you will give to our produce, no matter how largely you are prepared to approach Free Trade between different parts of the British Empire, it is no use your coming to us and asking for anything in return, because our fiscal system, strictly interpreted by the mandate of the constituencies, will not allow us to give you anything." In the second place, we might say, “If you want to do any service to us which is likely to arouse any kind of animosity or opposition on the part of any foreign country, we are bound to tell you that we cannot help you; there is nothing that we can do to bring that foreign country to its bearings and to secure the defence of your interests. Lord H. Cecil said that no one could resent more than he the action taken by Germany in regard to Canada. I should regret any invidious reference to Germans, but I am obliged to refer to Germany because it is the only country which has taken any hostile notice of these preferential arrangements. Germany alone has penalised Canada to the extent of a very large additional duty, because Canada has freely and voluntarily given to English products this preferential treatment. Apparently Lord H. Cecil thinks it is sufficient to say that we are a people who remember for a long period, and that some day or other we shall catch Germany in a hole. (Laughter.) That may be very good, but does he think that Canada is likely to be satisfied with that? (Hear, hear.) What has happened? Canada gave us this preference five years ago, and for five years she has been penalised. We have been bearing hot resentment in our bosom – (laughter) – but much good that does to Canada. Whatever else that may be, it is not business. (Ministerial cheers.) Suppose we had, in consequence of the decision of the country, to make that statement to our Colonies. I cannot ask [...] trymen, that it you make that reply to our Colonies, you must, in the first place, give up all hope of anything of the nature of closer fiscal relations with them and in the second place, in the absence of that, you must abandon altogether the idea of securing at any time a closer political relationship. If you have to abandon the idea of closer fiscal and political relations, then I repeat the opinion which I expressed at Birmingham, and say that a united Empire will be beyond the bounds of possibility. (Ministerial cheers.) It is my firm conviction, and it is because of the immense importance of that conviction that I ask the House to join eagerly in the discussion to which I invite them. Lord H. Cecil says he does not think, and cannot conceive, that it would be advisable to progress towards closer union by taking fiscal union first. All I can say is that the great example of the world is altogether opposed to the conclusion of my noble friend. How was the union of Germany effected? It was effected in the first instance by a Zollverein, and it could not have been achieved without a Zollverein, although, of course, processes of blood and iron also contributed largely to that welding –processes which, of course, my noble friend would not wish to see applied in the case of the Colonies. (Laughter.) Lord H. CECIL: Does the right hon. gentleman consider the case of England and Scotland? Mr. CHAMBERLAIN: I am quite prepared to consider that case and to admit that it is irrelevant to my argument. (Laughter.) I take it that this matter must come before the people of this country and that they will have to give an answer: (Ironical Opposition cheers.) I am perfectly certain they will give an answer for or against in no unmistakeable terms. (Renewed ironical Opposition cheers.) Hon. members opposite apparently think that the answer will be given in opposition to any change and therefore to raise this cry would be to them a great advantage. Under these circumstances I am sure they will be grateful to me for the services I have rendered them. (Laughter.) I shall make no electoral prophecy at the present time, but merely say that I have generally found the other side to be wrong. (Loud laughter.) Although I do not contradict or set up any alternative policy, I am bound to consider the possibility, at any rate, that the views of the nation may be in favour of some such change as indicated by this discussion. In that event, when we have got a mandate it will be time to produce a plan. A plan, in the sense of a definite and complete scheme, is absolutely impossible until we know a great deal concerning which we have still to inquire, and into which we cannot inquire profitably and advantageously unless we have got the country behind us. For instance, the first thing to be done is to consult the Colonies. Nothing could be worse than to negotiate with the Colonies and probably come to an agreement, only to find that at the next General Election it was rejected. I could conceive nothing more dangerous to union than that. Therefore, before we negotiate with the Colonies we must find out what, the opinion of the country is with regard to the principle at stake. If we had this mandate from the country the first thing that I should do in order to carry it out would be to consult the Colonies. In that case l should call another conference of the representatives of the self-governing Colonies, and I have not the slightest doubt myself that as the result arrangements which we should consider perfectly fair between the two parties – arrangements which gave us as much as we gave them – could be completed with all the Colonies. (Ministerial cheers.) That is my opinion. Against it let the House set the opinion of Sir C. Dilke. I really do not know what ground he has for pronouncing beforehand the opinion of Australia as a whole. (Hear, hear.) It is a very difficult thing for me, or for him, to anticipate beforehand what out [...] that that would not be the slightest advantage to them. Assume that statement to be correct, does he think that we should be such fools as to offer the Australians something which would not be of any advantage to them, and expect them, in return, to alter their system and give up Protection in our favour? Obviously, this must be matter for negotiation. Then comes Lord H. Cecil with a suggestion that if we are going to make these treaties of peace and commerce with our Colonies irritation will be aroused in other countries, and nothing will be more likely to promote disunion. That is merely an argument against making any treaty at all, and that we must never propose a treaty with our children for fear that, in the course of the negotiations, we might fail to come to an agreement. For myself, I should not have the slightest fear of entering on such negotiations. In order that a conference of this kind may discuss matters we must know from our own people not only what they can give but what they want in return. I want to have the information from every manufacturing district in this country, and through the chambers of commerce, who are everywhere taking the matter up, I hope to have it soon. (Ministerial cheers.) I want to know from them what particular articles of manufacture produced in their district could be more largely sold if, preferential rates were given in the Colonies, and what the extent of those preferential rates should be. The House will see that all this will necessary take time, and to claim that we should without this information, and before we have got anything in the nature of an expression of general agreement by the people of this country, put a plan before the House in the shape of a series of draft treaties with ill the Colonies, seems to be the height of absurdity and is absolutely impossible. (Cheers.) Mr. LOUGH: What are we to give? (Opposition cheers.) Mr. CHUCHILL: The right hon. gentleman says he welcomes discussion on this question, but how can we discuss it until we know what the plan is? (Opposition cheers.) Mr. CHAMBERLAIN: I have shown pretty clearly that anything in the nature of a detailed plan cannot be put before the House. But it does not need much acumen to ascertain what are the general lines upon which any arrangement of this kind must fall. I should have thought it was hardly necessary for me to explain them. (Ironical Opposition cheers.) But I wil – (Ministerial cheers) – as Mr. Lough has not been able to gather them himself. (Cheers and laughter) I have said that I conceive it to be possible to make preferential arrangements with the Colonies which will be beneficial to both sides, but if there is to the reciprocal preferences it is clear that we must not only receive, but have something to give. It is clear also that what we have to give must be given upon some great product of the Colonies, and as Mr. Lloyd-George, with greater perspicacity than Mr. Lough, can perceive, the preference must be given either on raw material or upon food, or upon both! (Ironical Opposition cheers and laughter.) That is pretty simple, I should have thought, but the Opposition take it as a great discovery. (Ministerial cheer and laughter.) I will carry it one step further, but I must say that when Mr. Lloyd-George attributes, some sentiments to me I do not accept his quotation as correct. He said I was in favour of taxing raw material and food. Of course, he had no right whatever from anything I have said to say anything of the sort. I am of opinion – it is only a personal opinion, and do not let me be told afterwards that I am laying down some law of the Medes and Persians by which I am to be governed, because the inquiry which must be instituted may throw further light on the subject. (Opposition laughter, and Ministerial cries of "Order!") I can quite understand the attitude of the Opposition by an allusion to further light on the subject. Hon. gentleman opposite would be glad to make light of it. (Ministerial cheers.) Mr. LAWSON WALTON: Did not the Prime Minister tell us that it was not intended to levy a tax on raw material or food? Mr. BALFOUR: Oh! no. MR. CHAMBERLAIN: No. Without binding myself for all time – (Opposition cries of " Oh!” and Mr. W. Redmond: Of course not!) – I must say this is extremely discourteous. (Ministerial cheers.) Without binding myself for all time, or shutting my eyes to possible fresh or further information, as far as I can see it will not be possible to put a tax at all on raw materials, and that for obvious reasons. It would be very difficult to find raw materials suitable for the purpose, and if a tax was put on raw materials it would be accompanied by drawbacks on finished exports, and although that is not at all impossible, because every country does it, it is a complicated system which, I think, can be dealt with in a much more simple way. We come to this, if you are going to give a preference – I do not say you are – you must make a tax on food. (Ironical Opposition cheers.) I make hon. gentlemen opposite a present of that, und I am prepared to go into any workman's or labourer's house in this country, and to address meetings of workmen and labourers, and, taking certain hypothetical calculations for my guide, as, for instance, assume a shilling or two shillings on corn, go to them and say, "Now then, this policy, if it is carried out, will cost you so much a week more than you are paying today for your food.” Mr. BALFOUR: Assuming that he pays it. Mr. CHAMBERLAIN: Yes, putting aside any economic question as to whether they would or would not pay the whole of any duty imposed, my argument would be: “I will assume that you pay every penny of the duty, and having assumed that, I would tell you what your cost will be. I know how many loaves you consume, I know how much meat you eat, I know what you take of this, that, and the other, on which it may be proposed to put a duty, and I will give to you a table from which you can tell for yourself how much extra wages you must get in order to cover the extra expenses of living? (Cheers.) There is the argument to which hon. members opposite will have to give their serious attention. (Opposition cheers.) If they can show that the whole of this business will mean a greater cost of living to the working-man and no increase of income, I have not the least doubt whatever that all their most optimistic prophecies will come true. But if I can show that in return for what I ask I will give more than I take, then, Ithink, poorly as they may regard my judgment, I may still have a chance. (Ministerial laughter.) That suggests another issue. Suppose you put a duty, not for the purpose of Protection at all, but for the purpose of gaining these advantages, and having something to give to your Colonies you put a duty on these products. I suppose it would produce a very large revenue. We do not want it for the normal expenditure of the country. Therefore we should have a large sum at our disposal. To whom shall we give that sum? In the first place, who is going to pay this tax? The working-classes are going to pay three-fourths of it. That is the calculation that on all taxation on consumption the working-classes pay three-fourths and the well-to-do one-fourth. That being so, according to my mind, as a matter of common justice the working-classes are entitled to every penny of the three-fourths, and I would give them without hesitation the other quarter, because I have always held, and it has been part of my speeches on this subject of social reform, that, while it would be absolute confiscation to put the cost of social reform solely on the shoulders of one class, und that the richer class the minority get, on the other hand, it is fair and right that they should make a contribution in return for the indirect advantages they gain from the contentment and prosperity of the working-classes. Therefore I should consider that any Government which imposed these duties, in addition to all the collateral advantages to which I have referred, would have a very large sum at their disposal which they ought and which they must apply to social reform. That led me to say the other day, when unexpectedly speaking on the subject, that old-age pensions, or anything else which cost large sums of money, which have hitherto seemed to be out of reach of immediate practical politics, would become practicable if this policy were carried out. (Ministerial cheers.) That is another argument which hon. members opposite will have to meet When I am talking to a working man and asking him to compare the advantages and disadvantages, another argument – I tell it you in anticipation – will be that that not only will you get back any benefits intended entirely and alone for you – the whole sum paid by you – but von will get back also that paid by the richer classes. That may of may not have any influence in the controversy; but, at all events, the working-classes, in addition to any direct advantages they may get through increased trade and increased wages, will be enabled to press upon the attention of this House a good number of social reforms which at present cannot be considered with any advantage. (Ministerial cheers.) I have said that this tax is not intentionally protective, but I do not want to deny, incidentally, in so far as it goes, that it is protective. (Opposition cheers.) That is to say, yon cannot put a duty on corn beyond a certain amount. I know that some people contest the question strongly how much of a duty is protective or not. Still, I would say it will be generally admitted if you put a considerable duty on corn that would be to a certain extent protection for the farmer. Although that is not the intention, it is the consequence of the tax. (Ministerial cheers.) There is no doubt whatever that the state of agriculture has been, and is, a serious question for this country. The continued reduction of our home food supply is a matter which has been found of so much importance as to justify the appointment of a special Commission, and it is perfectly clear that anything which increases our home food supply would have some advantages that might be set against any disadvantages which accompany protection of articles of food. There is this other question – how are we to defend our Colonies? How are we to operate in this case of Germany, for instance? We have already made representation after representation to the German Government with reference to the Canadian tariff, but this Government has not felt itself able to do anything for our own Colony. I do not see how the German Government can do anything until the German people find out that they cannot wreak their vengeance on Canada without suffering in their own pockets. But then, again, do not let my noble friend go off with the idea that if I had a mind to deal with this question I would go to. Germany and clap on a big duty on every German product, and make this a protected country to the extent of every import Germany sent here. Not at all. I should go to Germany as a negotiator, and say to them: "If you cannot meet us in this, I am afraid I shall have to put a duty on that.” (Ministerial cheers and laughter.) It would not be necessary to affect the whole trade with Germany. It would affect certain articles, and, of course, I should have to consider where we could put on these duties with the least danger to ourselves, and bring home most effectively so the German mind the impolicy of their conduct. Mr. W. REDMOND: You could refuse to collect Germany’s debts for them in future. (A laugh.) Mr. CHAMBERLAIN: I will remind the hon. member that Ireland has perhaps suffered even more than England. It has been a commonplace of Irish orators, especially of the Nationalist party, that it was owing, to the violence and oppression of this country that, Free Trade was imposed upon Ireland, and which has caused the destruction of Irish agriculture. While England as a great commercial country has benefited, Ireland has suffered out of all proportion. I say incidentally that it is clear this question will be interesting to Mr. W. Redmond's constituents. I need not elaborate that point more than is necessary. It is absolutely necessary that we should have the power to put duties on certain things if we are to retaliate in any way where our Colonies are injured by the reprisals of foreign countries. There is only one other point which will have to be considered. Is it not conceivable that we shall have to defend our own trade against unjust competition not against free exchange of commodities or of their natural price, but against something which I believe is absolutely new, and to which I am afraid insufficient, attention has been given at the present time? Has the House considered the practical working of the great trusts which are now being formed in America, in Germany, and on the Continent? These enormous aggregations of capital, wielded by a single brain, which can be brought to bear in the way of destroying a particular industry in this country without running any risk whatever? We are the one open market of the world. We are the one dumping-ground of the world. (Loud Ministerial cheers.) Let me try to make clear what happens. Suppose a manufacturer sells goods to the extent of £50,000 a year, and makes a profit of £5,000. His fixed expenses would be probably £6,000. But now if he can increase his business, and sell £100,000, his profits will be not merely £10,000, but they will be added to by the reduction of the fixed expenses on the second £50,000. His profits on £100,000, instead of being £10,000, might probably be £15,000. The result of that would be that he could afford io sell, as compared with his previous condition, his second £100,000, not only without profits, but even at a loss. That is what is happening in Germany and in America. In America the manufacturers are making and building up their works, and when there is a boom, as there has been recently, the works are at once increased. So long as the home trade will take all the works make, that is a most profitable arrangement for the manufacturer. No goods come to this country. But the moment there is a depression, say, in the iron trade, there is not the slightest doubt – it has been stated publicly by the president of that tremendous steel and iron corporation, and it is being actually done at this moment by the great German trust – great quantities of iron will be put down in this country and the countries we are supplying at a price we cannot possibly contest. (Ministerial cheers.) (An Hon. Member: So much the better.) The hon. member who is engaged in a different line of business has no objection whatever to the manufacturers being ruined. He says, indeed, “So much the better?” Well, I say this result will occur, inasmuch as no manufacturer hers can possibly stand a loss of that description for many years together; his business would be ruined, and the whole of the capital lost, as well as the profit. Of one thing I am certain, that, in spite of any decision that might be come to when this matter is raised, if there should be depression in some of our greatest industries, and this result which I predict should follow, nothing would prevent the people of this country from immediately imposing a duty which would defend them against any unfair competition. (Ministerial cheers.) I have indicated, at all events, the lines of the movement, und I have indicated the discussion which I wish to raise, and which I promise I will raise before the constituencies. (Ministerial cheers) Mr. LOUGH thought the honesty and candour of the Colonial Secretary were greatly to be praised. Mr. CHURCHILL had heard the statement of the Colonial Secretary with profound regret. He could not say that a system of preferential tariffs could inspire the House or the Conservative party with any enthusiasm, and still less the method by which that system could alone be carried into effect. The question would raise one of the greatest controversies of history. (Opposition cheers.) If they once started they could not stop at a simple system of a preferential character. The manufacturers of the country would support the Colonial Secretary, but they would insist in return upon the only tangible return – the establishment of an elaborate und complicated system of bounties and duties. (Opposition cheers.) That meant a vast and fundamental change not only in the character of political parties, but in the character of English public life. (Opposition cheers.) The old Conservative party, with its deep religions convictions, would fade away, and in its place they would see a party not perhaps unlike the Republican party in the United States; a party rich, ambitious, secular, materialist, whose elections would turn on tariff and whose members would be champions of individual trade interests. They would see the lobby of the House of Commons crowded with the touts of industries. (Opposition cheers.) Where was the overwhelming case for the change? Never was the wealth of the country greater; never were the trade returns higher; never did the income-tax produce more money; never was the loyalty of our Colonies more pronounced. (Opposition cheers.). Was the Government tired of these good, days? (Loud Opposition cheers.) There was no Colonial demand for the change, and no popular movement; but he did not know what popular movement the Colonial Secretary, with his immense popularity and unflinching courage, might not be able to excite. (Opposition cheers.) Mr. W. REDMOND could not understand the object of the Colonial Secretary in introducing the subject unless it be to wreck the Government. (Opposition cheers.) Mr. HARWOOD declared that if there had ever been a message which would rouse the blood of the Opposition, it was that which the Colonial Secretary had delivered. Mr. PEMBERTON considered that the terms of Mr. Chamberlain's speech must be put forward in future as the Unionist programme. He did not think it possible to express any opinion at present, but he did not wish it to be supposed that all the members of the Unionist party, because they had been members of that party in the past, necessarily approved of this programme. (Opposition cheers.) He admitted that much might be said in favour of it, but Unionist members would approach it with freedom. (Mr. Balfour: Hear, hear.) Mr. LABOUCHERE asked Mr. Balfour to gratify a somewhat legitimate anxiety on that side of the House by answering this question: Were the views expressed by the Colonial Secretary his own, or were they the views of the Cabinet? (Hear, hear.) The SPEAKER, at 7.15, put the question that the House adjourn till “August 8.“ (Cries of "June” and laughter.) The right hon. gentleman having given effect to the correction, the House immediately adjourned.

IMPORTANT DECLARATIONS BY THE PRIME MINISTER AND MR. CHAMBERLAIN A MANDATE INVITED. RAW MATERIALS FREE On the motion for the adjournment of the House of Commons for the Whitsuntide recess yesterday, Sir Charles Dilke, in the absence of the leaders of the Liberal party – on which the Prime Minister commented – called attention to Mr. Chamberlain's speech on preferential trade, within the Empire. The declarations of Mr. Balfour and Mr. Chamberlain were of the most decisive and important character. The policy outlined is this: The subject having been unanimously brought to the attention of the Imperial Government at last year’s conference by the Colonial Premiers, it was Mr. Chamberlain’s duty to raise the discussion. When a dissolution occurs, the subject to be submitted to the judgement of the electorate will be: The advisability of reciprocal trade between the Mother Country and the Colonies, which would Leave raw material for manufacture free. Place a tax on food, and with the product of such impost carry out desired but at present unattainable, social reforms. The objects to be kept in view were: (1) The power to retaliate against foreign countries which penalise British Colonies for giving preference to the United Kingdom, thus treating each Colony as a separate nation in spite of Imperial protests. (2) The binding of the Empire closer together in the bonds of reciprocal trade. The course of events indicated by the Colonial Secretary is this: First. The principle –not a fixed plan – of preferential trade must receive the verdict of the country for or against. "I promise I will raise the question before the constituencies, Mr. Chamberlain declared, after speaking for fifty minutes. Secondly. I the country gives a mandate a Colonial Conference will be called to reduce the principle to a definite plan. Mr. Chamberlain elaborated further his idea that fiscal reform must go hand in hand with social reform – old-age pensions, for example. Any tax due to preferential treatment of the Colonies, and to enable the United Kingdom to negotiate trade treaties with foreign Powers, with greater advantage, would probably be on food. Taxes on articles of consumption are paid for three parts by the working classes and one part by the well-to-do. In return, all the product of the taxation – not three-quarters, merely – would be devoted to social reform – it might be old-age pensions – which would be thus brought within the reach of the nation, and in addition, in Mr. Chamberlain's view, the working classes would benefit by increased trade and increased wages. Incidentally, agriculture in Great Britain, and also in Ireland, would derive advantage from the scheme. In the course of his speech, which preceded that of the Colonial Secretary, Mr. Balfour admitted that they had to face two difficulties which were great: (1) The traditional objection of our population to a tax on food. (2) The traditional affection of the Colonies for a system of protection. The Prime Minister pointed out that the question was not one that the House “would have to decide this Session, or next Session, or the Session after that – thus silencing Lobby rumours of an early Dissolution – but it was a question of general fiscal policy which required the most careful examination and study on its strictly economic side, and also on its Imperial and social side.” Concluding, the Prime Minister said amid loud Ministerial cheers – and the words are significant and weighty: If public opinion ripens, if the Colonies and if the people of this country are of opinion that we ought to do something to put the British Empire in an economic position which will make it in any way equal to the magnificent economic position obtained by the United States, I think we shall have done well. I am not certain that this scheme is practicable, but I am certain that unless this scheme proves to be practicable, or unless some other scheme having the same results, can be brought to fruition – if the British Empire is to remain as it is at present, a series of isolated economic units – it is vain for us to hope that this branch, at all events, of the great Anglo-Saxon race is destined to have the great and triumphant economic progress which undoubtedly lies before the United States of America. Unwonted excitement prevailed in the Lobby after the brilliant speeches of Mr. Balfour and Mr. Chamberlain in the House of Commons on the great question of preferential trade within the Empire. Members on all sides recognised that the utterances of the Prime Minister and the Colonial Secretary were not only notable in themselves, but might be fraught with far-reaching political and party consequences. Radicals, as might have been expected, were loud in their condemnation of the new policy. Some Unionists, particularly those associated with manufacturing and industrial centres, shook their heads dubiously over the situation, but a majority of the Ministerialists were delighted beyond measure at the prospect of having a popular rallying cry for the next general election. “It is the pluckiest thing in politics!“ “ It is the greatest fiscal revolution of our time!“ “It will give fresh life and vigour to the Unionist party!” – these were the exclamations heard in many quarters. One thing was established beyond doubt that the debate was raised without the sanction of the official Opposition. All the leaders were absent from the front bench, and their absence was not unintentional. Having arranged for a full-dress discussion on the second reading of the Finance Bill, they were indignant at the attempt to cut the ground from under their feet, and kept away as a protest against the conduct of their lieutenants. “There is very good reason,“ remarked an ex-Cabinet Minister, “why we should stay away. No division can be taken to-day, whereas we intend to insist upon one, so that the public may know how members vote on this vital issue.”
